newsitem.title: INDIA: Bank of India gives maiden 15 pct div.
newsitem.headline: Bank of India gives maiden 15 pct div.

text.p: State-run Bank of India Ltd (BOI) announced a maiden dividend of 15 percent on Thursday, three months after listing on the Bombay Stock Exchange.
"After just three months of trading, we have announced a dividend of 15 percent. We expect an even better reward next year," BOI's chairman and managing director, M.G. Bhide told reporters in Bombay.
"We have the highest recorded profit of any nationalised bank, and that too after deducting public listing expenses of 327.6 million rupees," he said.
BOI raised 6.7 billion rupees through an initial public offering in March this year.
Bhide said he expected a growth of 20 percent in operating profit in 1997/98 (April-March).
"We are targeting a figure of 6.3 billion rupees as operating profit, on the back of 20.5 percent growth in deposits."
BOI announced its 1996/97 results earlier on Thursday.
The bank's net profit climbed to 3.6 billion rupees from 2.76 billion in 1995/96 while its income rose to 40.04 billion rupees from 33.11 billion rupees the previous year.
Bhide said BOI was planning to expand several of its existing businesses and enter new ones. He said credit cards was one area BOI would be venturing into.
Housing finance was another area the bank was looking at, he added.
BOI is also planning to expand its overseas presence, he said.

"Close to 21 percent of our profits come from foreign operations. And for the second consecutive year, all our foreign offices, apart from our Jakarta representative office, have made profits," Bhide said.
BOI has 18 foreign branches, and is in the process of adding a few more in the Middle East and one in Trinidad and Tobago.

BOI's chairman admitted that the bank needed to raise long-term debt to the tune of 8 billion to 10 billion rupees. He said the bank was considering several options for this, including an issue of Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs).
"While we need to raise this debt, we want to make sure that we are not over-capitalised," he added.
